stimuli.title: Heart Rate and Running Speed
stimuli.html:
A sports science lab tested how running speed affects heart rate. Three volunteers of similar age and fitness each ran on a treadmill for 4 minutes at each speed, resting for 10 minutes between stages. A chest-strap monitor recorded each volunteer's heart rate at the end of every 4-minute stage. The treadmill was kept level (0% incline), and the room was kept at 20 °C for every stage.

stimuli.title: Muscle Fiber Types
stimuli.html:
Skeletal muscles contain two main types of muscle fibers.

Slow-twitch fibers contract slowly and with less force, but they can keep working for a long time without tiring. They contain many mitochondria and have a rich blood supply. They rely mainly on aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen to break down glucose and fats completely and releases a large amount of ATP, the cell's usable energy.

Fast-twitch fibers contract quickly and powerfully, but they tire within seconds to a minute or two. They have fewer mitochondria and rely heavily on anaerobic processes, which break down glucose without oxygen. Anaerobic breakdown is fast, but it releases far less ATP from each glucose molecule and produces lactate.

The table shows typical approximate percentages of slow-twitch fibers in the thigh muscle of three groups of adults.

stimuli.title: Flower Color in Snapdragons
stimuli.html:
In snapdragon plants, flower color shows incomplete dominance: neither allele completely hides the other. A plant with two alleles for red (RR) has red flowers, a plant with two alleles for white (WW) has white flowers, and a plant with one of each allele (RW) has pink flowers.

A gardener crosses two pink-flowered plants (RW × RW). The Punnett square below sets up the cross.

stimuli.title: Coral Bleaching Survey
stimuli.html:
Reef-building corals get most of their food from tiny algae that live inside their tissues. When ocean water stays unusually warm, corals can lose these algae and turn white, an event called bleaching.

Marine biologists surveyed the same reef at the end of five different summers. For each summer, they recorded how many weeks the water stayed at least 1 °C above the reef's usual summer maximum, and the percent of coral colonies that were bleached.

stimuli.title: A Kelp Forest Food Web
stimuli.html:
Giant kelp is a large brown seaweed that grows in cold, shallow coastal waters along the Pacific coast of North America, forming underwater "forests." The list below describes some feeding relationships in a kelp forest. Each arrow means "is eaten by."

  • Giant kelp → sea urchins
  • Giant kelp → abalone (a large sea snail)
  • Sea urchins → sea otters
  • Abalone → sea otters
  • Phytoplankton → zooplankton
  • Zooplankton → small fish
  • Small fish → harbor seals
  • Sea otters → orcas
  • Harbor seals → orcas

During the fur trade of the 1700s and 1800s, sea otters were hunted until they had nearly disappeared from much of this coast. In many places, sea urchin populations then grew very large, and the urchins grazed the kelp down to bare rock, leaving areas known as "urchin barrens." In places where sea otters later returned, urchin numbers fell and kelp forests grew back. Because sea otters have such a large effect on their ecosystem compared with their numbers, ecologists call them a keystone species.

stimuli.title: Osmosis in Potato Cells
stimuli.html:
Water moves across cell membranes by osmosis, from a region where water is more concentrated (fewer dissolved particles) to a region where water is less concentrated (more dissolved particles).

Students cut five identical cylinders from the same potato and measured the mass of each. They placed each cylinder in a different salt solution for 24 hours, then blotted it dry and measured its mass again.

Salt concentration of solution (%)01234
Change in mass of potato (%)+9.0+3.5−1.5−6.0−8.5

stimuli.title: Armor Plates in Stickleback Fish
stimuli.html:
Threespine sticklebacks are small fish that live both in the ocean and in many freshwater lakes. Most ocean sticklebacks have a full row of bony armor plates along each side, which helps protect them from large predatory fish. A few ocean sticklebacks carry an allele that produces a low-plate form with only a few plates.

Researchers studied a lake that was colonized by ocean sticklebacks. The lake has few large predatory fish, and in this lake, low-plate fish tend to grow faster and reach breeding size sooner than fully plated fish. The researchers sampled the lake's sticklebacks every five years.

Years after colonization051015

stimuli.title: Momentum in a Tackle
stimuli.html:
During a football practice, a 90 kg player running east at 6 m/s tackles a 75 kg ball carrier who is standing still. The two players hold onto each other and move together as one unit right after the tackle.

Momentum is found with p = mv, where m is mass in kilograms and v is velocity in meters per second. In a collision, the total momentum of the objects just before the collision equals their total momentum just after it.

stimuli.title: Basketball Bounce and Temperature
stimuli.html:
A student tested whether temperature affects how high a basketball bounces. She inflated four identical basketballs to the same air pressure at room temperature. She then stored each ball for 2 hours at a different temperature. Right after removing each ball, she dropped it from a height of 1.8 m onto the same gym floor and measured how high it bounced. She repeated each drop three times and recorded the mean.

Storage temperature (°C)−552035
Mean bounce height (m)0.921.041.181.26

stimuli.title: Cold Packs and Hand Warmers
stimuli.html:
Athletic trainers often use instant cold packs on injuries. A cold pack contains water and a separate pouch of solid ammonium nitrate. Squeezing the pack breaks the pouch, and the ammonium nitrate dissolves in the water. This process absorbs energy from the surroundings, so the pack quickly feels cold.

Fans at winter games often use hand warmers. A hand warmer contains fine iron powder. When the package is opened, the iron reacts with oxygen from the air to form iron(III) oxide, and the reaction releases energy as heat. The unbalanced equation is:

Fe + O2 → Fe2O3

A process that absorbs energy from its surroundings is endothermic. A process that releases energy to its surroundings is exothermic.

stimuli.title: Mapping the Seafloor with Sonar
stimuli.html:
A research ship maps the depth of the seafloor with sonar. The ship sends a pulse of sound straight down and measures the time until the echo returns. The sound travels down to the seafloor and back up, so the echo time covers twice the depth. Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 m/s.

LocationEcho time (s)Depth (m)

The ship's sonar pulse has a frequency of 12,000 Hz. For any wave, wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = fλ).

stimuli.title: Tides at a Coastal Town
stimuli.html:
Ocean tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, with a smaller pull from the Sun. Most coastlines have two high tides and two low tides in a little more than 24 hours. When the Sun, Earth, and Moon are lined up (at new moon and full moon), their pulls combine, producing spring tides with very high high tides and very low low tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other (at first quarter and third quarter moon), they partly cancel, producing neap tides with a smaller difference between high and low tide.

items.prompt: In this experiment, what is the dependent variable?
options: The volunteers' heart rate at the end of each stage
items.explain:
The dependent variable is what the researchers measure to see whether it responds to the change they make. They measured heart rate at the end of each stage.

Treadmill speed is the independent variable, because the researchers deliberately changed it. The incline (0%) and room temperature (20 °C) were kept the same, so they are controlled variables.

items.prompt: What is the mean heart rate of the three volunteers at a speed of 10 km/h? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Mean = sum of the values ÷ number of values.

140 + 146 + 137 = 423
423 ÷ 3 = 141 beats per minute

Divide by 3, the number of volunteers, not by 5 (the number of speeds tested).

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: As running speed increased, the volunteers' mean heart rate increased.
Doubling the running speed doubled the mean heart rate.
Heart rate would keep rising without limit at speeds faster than 12 km/h.
The rise in heart rate was caused mainly by changes in room temperature.
items.explain:
The mean heart rate rose at every step: 64 → 99 → 121 → 141 → 163 beats per minute as speed went from 0 to 12 km/h. So heart rate increased as running speed increased.

Doubling speed from 6 to 12 km/h raised the mean from 99 to 163, not to 198, so heart rate did not double. The study tested only speeds up to 12 km/h, so it gives no evidence about much faster speeds. Room temperature was held at 20 °C, so it could not have caused the change.

items.prompt:
Complete the explanation of why heart rate rises during faster running.

Working leg muscles need more {{0}} to carry out cellular respiration. The heart beats faster to deliver it, and the {{1}} system increases the breathing rate to take in more of it and to get rid of more {{2}}, a waste product of cellular respiration.
items.explain:
Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). Faster running uses more energy, so muscles need more oxygen.

The circulatory system (heart and blood) delivers the oxygen, and the respiratory system (lungs) brings it into the body. Breathing faster also removes more carbon dioxide, which is a product, not a raw material, of cellular respiration.

The digestive system supplies glucose from food, but it does not control breathing rate or gas exchange.

items.skill: Applying information to a new situation
items.prompt: A test shows that an athlete's thigh muscle is about 78% slow-twitch fibers. Based on the passage, in which event is this athlete most likely to perform best?
items.explain:
Slow-twitch fibers resist fatigue and rely on aerobic respiration, so they suit long-lasting effort. The table shows elite marathon runners average about 80% slow-twitch fibers. A 78% slow-twitch athlete is best matched to a long endurance event such as the 10,000-meter run.

The 100-meter dash, shot put, and high jump are short, explosive events that depend on fast, powerful contractions, which come from fast-twitch fibers. Elite sprinters average only about 25% slow-twitch fibers.

items.prompt:
Which statements about slow-twitch fibers are supported by the passage?

Select two answers.
options: They rely mainly on aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen.
They tire within seconds to a minute or two.
They rely mainly on anaerobic processes that produce lactate.
They contract with more force than fast-twitch fibers.
items.explain:
The passage states that slow-twitch fibers contain many mitochondria and rely mainly on aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen and releases a large amount of ATP.

Tiring within seconds, relying on anaerobic processes, producing lactate, and contracting with more force are all traits the passage gives to fast-twitch fibers.

items.prompt: Complete the Punnett square for the cross RW × RW. What percent of the offspring are expected to have pink flowers?
items.explain:
Combine one allele from each parent:

RW
RRRRW
WRWWW

Pink flowers come only from RW, which fills 2 of the 4 boxes: 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50 = 50%.

A common error is answering 75%, as if one allele were dominant. With incomplete dominance, RR plants are red, not pink, so only the RW boxes count.

items.prompt: The gardener wants a cross in which every offspring has pink flowers. Which cross should she make?
items.explain:
In RR × WW, the red parent can pass on only R, and the white parent can pass on only W. Every offspring is RW, so 100% are pink.

RW × RW gives 25% red, 50% pink, 25% white. RW × WW gives 50% pink and 50% white. RR × RW gives 50% red and 50% pink.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the survey data?
options: Coral colonies bleach only when the water is above normal for at least 8 weeks.
Water temperature has no effect on coral bleaching.
Longer periods of above-normal water temperature were linked to a greater percent of bleached colonies.
Half of all coral colonies bleach after any period of warm water.
items.explain:
As the number of weeks of above-normal temperature rose (0, 2, 4, 6, 8), the percent of bleached colonies rose every time (3%, 10%, 28%, 51%, 74%). So longer warm periods were linked to more bleaching.

Bleaching happened in every summer, even with 0 or 2 weeks of warm water, so it does not require 8 weeks. The steady rise shows that temperature is linked to bleaching. Only Summer D (6 weeks) came close to half; after 2 weeks, only 10% bleached.

items.prompt: Read the description of coral and algae below. Click the sentence that best explains why a bleached coral may die if the warm water continues.
spans: Reef-building corals are animals that live together with tiny algae inside their tissues.
The algae use sunlight to carry out photosynthesis, and they share much of the sugar they make with the coral.
In return, the coral gives the algae a protected place to live and supplies carbon dioxide and nutrients.
When the water stays unusually warm for several weeks, the coral expels the algae and its tissue turns pale or white.
Without the algae, the coral loses its main source of food and begins to starve.
If the water cools soon enough, the algae can return and the coral can recover.
items.explain:
The coral depends on sugar made by the algae. The sentence "Without the algae, the coral loses its main source of food and begins to starve" explains why a bleached coral may die if the algae stay gone.

The sentence about the coral expelling the algae describes what bleaching is, not why it can be deadly. The last sentence describes recovery, not death.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, which sequence of events most likely followed the near disappearance of sea otters?
options: Sea urchin populations increased, and the amount of kelp decreased.
Sea urchin populations decreased, and the amount of kelp increased.
Orca populations increased, and sea urchin populations decreased.
Phytoplankton populations decreased, and harbor seal populations increased.
items.explain:
Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. With few otters left, fewer urchins were eaten, so urchin populations grew and the urchins grazed the kelp down, creating urchin barrens. The passage describes exactly this result.

The reverse (fewer urchins, more kelp) is what happened where otters returned. Orcas eat otters, so losing otters would not increase orcas. Phytoplankton and harbor seals are in a separate food chain that does not depend on otters in this web.

items.prompt: Use the feeding relationships in the kelp forest to classify each organism. Drag each one into the correct category.
items.explain:
Producer: Giant kelp makes its own food by photosynthesis.

Primary consumers: Sea urchins eat kelp, and zooplankton eat phytoplankton; both eat producers.

Secondary consumer: Sea otters eat sea urchins and abalone, which are primary consumers.

Tertiary consumer: Harbor seals eat small fish, which eat zooplankton (primary consumers). So small fish are secondary consumers and harbor seals are tertiary consumers.

A common mistake is placing harbor seals with sea otters because both are marine mammals; what matters is how many feeding steps separate each one from the producer.

items.prompt: At one salt concentration, the potato would neither gain nor lose mass, because water would move into and out of the cells at the same rate. Based on the data, about what is that salt concentration?
items.explain:
The mass change crosses zero between 1% (+3.5%) and 2% (−1.5%), so the answer is between 1% and 2%.

Over that 1-point step, the mass change drops by 3.5 − (−1.5) = 5.0 percentage points. To fall from +3.5 to 0 takes 3.5 ÷ 5.0 = 0.7 of the step.
1 + 0.7 = about 1.7%

At 2.5%, the potato would already be losing mass (between −1.5% and −6.0%). At 0.5%, it would still be gaining mass, because water moves into cells placed in a solution with fewer dissolved particles than the cells.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the lake's stickleback population over 15 years?
options: Each fish lost some of its plates during its lifetime because it no longer needed them, and it passed this change to its offspring.
The lake water dissolved the bony plates of the fish that colonized the lake.
The researchers removed fully plated fish from the lake during each sample.
Low-plate fish, which were present from the start, grew and bred sooner in the lake, so the low-plate allele became more common with each generation.
items.explain:
This is natural selection. The passage says the low-plate allele was already present in a few ocean fish, and that in this lake low-plate fish grow faster and reach breeding size sooner. They left more offspring, so the low-plate form rose from 4% to 75%.

Individual fish do not lose plates because they "don't need them" and then pass that change on; traits acquired during a lifetime are not inherited. Nothing in the passage says the water dissolved plates or that researchers removed fish.

items.prompt: What was the sprinter's average speed for the whole 100-meter race? Round to the nearest tenth.
items.explain:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

100 m ÷ 10.4 s ≈ 9.615 m/s, which rounds to 9.6 m/s.

A common error is dividing time by distance (10.4 ÷ 100 = 0.104), which gives seconds per meter, not meters per second.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the sprinter's motion during the race?
options: She ran at a constant speed for the entire race.
She ran fastest during the first 20 meters and then slowed down.
She sped up during the first 60 meters and then ran at a nearly constant speed.
She slowed down steadily during the last 40 meters.
items.explain:
Find the time for each 20 m section:

0–20 m: 3.0 s (20 ÷ 3.0 ≈ 6.7 m/s)
20–40 m: 2.0 s (10.0 m/s)
40–60 m: 1.8 s (≈ 11.1 m/s)
60–80 m: 1.8 s (≈ 11.1 m/s)
80–100 m: 1.8 s (≈ 11.1 m/s)

Her speed increased through the first 60 m and then stayed the same, so she sped up and then held a nearly constant speed.

The first 20 m was her slowest section, because she started from rest. The last three sections took equal times, so she did not slow down.

items.prompt: What was the sprinter's average speed between the 60-meter mark and the 80-meter mark?
items.explain:
Distance for this section: 80 − 60 = 20 m
Time for this section: 8.6 − 6.8 = 1.8 s
Speed = 20 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 11.1 m/s

9.3 m/s is her average from the start to the 80 m mark (80 ÷ 8.6), not for this section alone. 0.09 m/s comes from dividing time by distance (1.8 ÷ 20). 20 m/s ignores the time and uses only the distance.

items.prompt: What is the momentum of the 90 kg player just before the tackle?
items.explain:
p = m × v
p = 90 kg × 6 m/s = 540 kg·m/s

15 comes from dividing mass by velocity (90 ÷ 6), and 96 from adding (90 + 6). 1,620 is the player's kinetic energy in joules (½ × 90 × 62), which is a different quantity.

items.prompt: What is the speed of the two players together just after the tackle? Round to the nearest tenth.
items.explain:
Total momentum before = 90 × 6 + 75 × 0 = 540 kg·m/s (the ball carrier is standing still).

After the tackle, both players move together, so the combined mass is 90 + 75 = 165 kg.

540 = 165 × v
v = 540 ÷ 165 ≈ 3.27 m/s, which rounds to 3.3 m/s.

A common error is dividing by only 75 kg (540 ÷ 75 = 7.2 m/s). Both players are moving after the tackle, so their masses must be added.

items.prompt: Which variable did the student keep the same for every ball so that the test would be fair?
options: The height from which each ball was dropped
The temperature at which each ball was stored
The mean bounce height of each ball
The air pressure inside each ball at the moment it was dropped
items.explain:
Every ball was dropped from 1.8 m, so drop height is a controlled variable. (The floor and the type of ball were also kept the same.)

Storage temperature was deliberately changed (independent variable), and bounce height was measured (dependent variable). The balls started at the same pressure at room temperature, but heating or cooling the air inside changed the pressure before each drop, so pressure at the moment of the drop was not kept the same.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the bouncing basketballs.

As a ball falls, its gravitational potential energy changes into {{0}} energy. No ball bounced back up to the full 1.8 m drop height, because during each bounce some energy was changed into {{1}} energy and sound. This does not break the law of conservation of energy, because the total amount of energy {{2}}.
items.explain:
A falling ball speeds up, so its stored gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy (energy of motion).

When the ball squashes against the floor, some energy becomes thermal energy (the ball and floor warm slightly) and sound. Less energy is left to lift the ball, so it bounces lower than 1.8 m.

Energy is changed from one form to another but never created or destroyed, so the total amount of energy stays the same. The "missing" energy has not been destroyed; it has spread out as heat and sound.

items.prompt: What is the density of Sample B, the deep ocean water? Enter your answer in g/mL as a decimal.
items.explain:
Density = mass ÷ volume
Density = 205.6 g ÷ 200.0 mL = 1.028 g/mL

A common error is dividing volume by mass (200.0 ÷ 205.6 ≈ 0.973), which gives a value lower than fresh water and makes no sense for cold, salty water.

items.prompt: A student carefully pours the four samples into a tall, clear tube so that they do not mix. Which sample will form the bottom layer, and which will form the top layer?
options: Sample D on the bottom and Sample B on top
Sample B on the bottom and Sample D on top
Sample A on the bottom and Sample C on top
Sample C on the bottom and Sample A on top
items.explain:
Denser liquids sink below less dense liquids. Ranked from most to least dense: B (1.028) > A (1.0235) > C (1.0045) > D (0.9970).

So Sample B, the cold, salty deep water, forms the bottom layer, and Sample D, the fresh water, floats on top.

Reversing the order is a common mistake. Samples A and C are in the middle layers, not at the top or bottom.

items.prompt:
Choose the coefficients that balance the equation for the hand-warmer reaction.

{{0}} Fe + {{1}} O2 → {{2}} Fe2O3
items.explain:
Balance oxygen first. O2 has 2 oxygen atoms and Fe2O3 has 3. The smallest number both 2 and 3 divide into is 6, so use 3 O2 (6 O) and 2 Fe2O3 (6 O).

Now 2 Fe2O3 contains 2 × 2 = 4 iron atoms, so use 4 Fe.

Check: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3 has 4 Fe and 6 O on each side. A common error is 2Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3, which leaves only 2 Fe on the left but 4 Fe on the right.

items.prompt: Classify each process as endothermic or exothermic. Drag each one into the correct category.
choices: Ammonium nitrate dissolving in a cold pack
Iron reacting with oxygen in a hand warmer
Ice melting in a cup of sports drink
Water vapor condensing into droplets on a cold water bottle
items.explain:
Endothermic: The cold pack absorbs energy from its surroundings (stated in the passage). Melting ice absorbs heat from the drink, which is why the drink gets colder.

Exothermic: The hand-warmer reaction releases heat (stated in the passage). Burning wood releases heat and light. Condensation releases energy as water vapor turns into liquid.

A common mistake is calling condensation endothermic because it happens on a cold surface. The cold bottle removes energy from the vapor; the vapor releases energy as it condenses, which slightly warms the bottle.

items.prompt: What is the depth of the seafloor at Location 2?
items.explain:
Distance the sound traveled = speed × time = 1,500 m/s × 5.6 s = 8,400 m.

That distance is down and back, so the depth is half: 8,400 ÷ 2 = 4,200 m.

Check with Location 1: 1,500 × 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1,500 m, which matches the table. 8,400 m forgets to divide by 2. 2,100 m divides by 4 instead of 2. 270 m comes from dividing 1,500 by 5.6.

items.prompt: What is the wavelength of the ship's sonar pulse in seawater?
items.explain:
v = f × λ, so λ = v ÷ f.

λ = 1,500 m/s ÷ 12,000 Hz = 0.125 m

8 m comes from dividing frequency by speed (12,000 ÷ 1,500). 18,000,000 m comes from multiplying instead of dividing. 13,500 m comes from adding the two numbers.

items.prompt: Sports drinks contain electrolytes such as sodium (Na) and potassium (K). Sodium and potassium are in the same group (column) of the periodic table and react with other elements in similar ways. Which statement best explains why?
options: They have the same number of protons.
They have the same atomic mass.
They have the same number of neutrons.
They have the same number of valence (outer-shell) electrons.
items.explain:
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons. Sodium and potassium each have 1 valence electron, which they easily give up, so they react in similar ways.

Each element has its own number of protons (sodium 11, potassium 19), which is what makes them different elements. Their atomic masses and neutron numbers also differ.

items.prompt: About how much time passed between the two high tides shown in the table?
items.explain:
The high tides were at 12:40 a.m. and 1:05 p.m.

12:40 a.m. to 12:40 p.m. = 12 hours
12:40 p.m. to 1:05 p.m. = 25 minutes
Total: 12 hours 25 minutes

About 6 hours 15 minutes is the time from a high tide to the next low tide. 24 hours 50 minutes is the time for two full tide cycles, not one.

items.prompt: About one week after the day shown, the Moon is at third quarter. Compared with the day shown, how will the difference between high tide and low tide most likely change?
options: The difference will be larger, because the Sun and Moon will be lined up with Earth.
The difference will stay the same, because tides are caused only by the Moon.
There will be no tides, because the Sun's pull will cancel the Moon's pull completely.
The difference will be smaller, because the Sun and Moon will pull at right angles to each other.
items.explain:
The day shown was a full moon, when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are lined up and spring tides occur. At third quarter, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel, producing neap tides with a smaller difference between high and low tide.

The Sun and Moon are lined up at full and new moon, not at third quarter. The passage says the Sun adds a smaller pull, so tides are not caused only by the Moon. The pulls only partly cancel, so tides continue.

items.prompt: The sentences below explain how hurricanes get their energy. Click the sentence that best explains why the storm in the table weakened on Days 4 and 5.
spans: Hurricanes form over tropical oceans where the surface water is at least about 26 °C.
Warm ocean water evaporates, and the warm, moist air rises.
As the water vapor condenses into clouds, it releases heat, which warms the surrounding air and makes it rise even faster.
Earth's rotation causes the rising, inflowing air to spin.
When a hurricane moves over land or over cooler water, it is cut off from its supply of warm, moist air, and it weakens.
Even after a storm weakens, it can still cause heavy flooding far inland.
items.explain:
The table shows the storm's center moved over land on Days 4 and 5, and its winds dropped from 210 to 150 to 85 km/h. The sentence "When a hurricane moves over land or over cooler water, it is cut off from its supply of warm, moist air, and it weakens" explains this.

The other sentences explain how hurricanes form or gain strength, or describe flooding after weakening, but they do not explain why the storm lost strength.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: The storm grew stronger as it passed over warmer water and weakened after it moved over land.
The storm's wind speed did not depend on where the storm's center was located.
The storm was strongest on the day it made landfall.
The storm weakened each day it was over the ocean.
items.explain:
Over the ocean, the sea surface temperature rose from 27 to 29 to 30 °C, and the maximum wind rose from 120 to 175 to 210 km/h. After landfall, the wind fell to 150 and then 85 km/h. So the storm strengthened over warmer water and weakened over land.

The storm was strongest on Day 3, the day before landfall, not on Day 4. Its wind speed rose, not fell, on each day over the ocean, and the clear change after landfall shows that location mattered.

items.prompt: Dublin, Ireland, and Saskatoon, Canada, are at about the same latitude (about 52–53° north). In January, Dublin's average temperature is about 5 °C, while Saskatoon's is about −15 °C. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?
options: Dublin is much closer to the equator than Saskatoon.
Dublin lies near the Atlantic Ocean, where a warm current carries heat from the tropics and the ocean keeps winter air mild, while Saskatoon lies far inland.
Saskatoon is at a much higher elevation, so its air is always colder than Dublin's.
Earth's tilt points Ireland toward the Sun in January while Canada points away.
items.explain:
Water holds heat well and changes temperature slowly, so places near the ocean have milder winters. A warm ocean current (the Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Current) carries heat from the tropics toward Ireland. Saskatoon, deep in the middle of North America, has no ocean nearby to moderate its winter.

The two cities are at about the same latitude, so neither is much closer to the equator. Both cities are in the Northern Hemisphere, so Earth's tilt affects them the same way in January. Saskatoon is only about 500 m above sea level, which is not enough to explain a 20 °C difference.

items.prompt: When it is winter in the United States, it is summer along Australia's Great Barrier Reef. What is the main reason?
options: The Sun gives off more energy in December and January.
The Southern Hemisphere has more ocean, and ocean water produces its own heat.
The Moon blocks some sunlight from reaching the Northern Hemisphere in winter.
In December and January, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so it receives more direct sunlight and longer days.
items.explain:
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. In December and January, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer. That brings summer to Australia while the Northern Hemisphere, tilted away, has winter.

The Sun's energy output does not change with Earth's seasons; if it did, both hemispheres would warm at the same time. Ocean water stores heat but does not produce it. The Moon does not block sunlight from a hemisphere for a season.
